content: Observers are individuals who are selected based on their expertise and knowledge of the onchocerciasis program in the applicant country. Their role is to provide technical input and advice to the International Verification Team (IVT) and to assist the WHO Secretariat in coordinating with national authorities to address any requests made by the IVT. However, observers must not directly contact national authorities without prior consultation with the WHO Secretariat. In certain cases, such as in densely populated countries, more than two observers may be required, and these may include regional program experts from initiatives like the Onchocerciasis Elimination Program for the Americas or the African Program for Onchocerciasis Control, which support the country’s elimination efforts. The WHO Secretariat is responsible for providing IVT members and observers with the necessary documentation, coordinating with national authorities to organize and arrange country visits if required, and ensuring the development, finalization, and submission of the IVT report. It is strongly recommended that all members, observers, and the Secretariat are fluent in the language of the dossier and the language commonly used in the applicant country. If the IVT determines that a visit to the applicant country is necessary for a thorough assessment, the WHO Secretariat will arrange the visit. It is suggested that such visits last at least five working days, though the duration may vary depending on the number of endemic areas (foci) to be visited. The purpose of the visit is to allow IVT members to familiarize themselves with the operations and personnel of the elimination program, evaluate the reliability of the country’s claims, and formulate conclusions and recommendations. The visit may be preceded by teleconferences involving IVT members, observers, and the WHO Secretariat to discuss requirements, needs, and the information to be reviewed during the visit. The methodology for the country visit should include the following steps: 1. Examination of the dossier and any other relevant documents related to the program. 2. Interviews with program personnel and technical staff involved in onchocerciasis control or elimination activities at both central and peripheral levels. 3. Interviews with community members living in one or more endemic areas, with a visit to at least one community in an endemic region being highly recommended. 4. Internal discussions among IVT members on the first day in the country to clarify procedures, address questions, and plan the visit. The chairperson of the IVT, selected from among its members, is responsible for structuring the meetings, regulating the contributions of observers, and ensuring that the procedures and timing of discussions are appropriate. The chairperson also represents the IVT in interactions with national authorities, alongside the WHO Secretariat. The IVT report should ideally be finalized and signed during the visit. If this is not possible, the report should be completed immediately after the visit. The original copy of the report must be forwarded by the relevant WHO Country Office to the WHO Director-General through the appropriate WHO Regional Office. Observers may be informed by the chairperson, after consultation with other members, whether they can participate in drafting and finalizing the report. If the national authorities of the applicant country request a debriefing before the team departs, preliminary information on the conclusions can be shared. However, it should be emphasized that the final decision will be made by the WHO Director-General, not the IVT. Press releases at this stage are strongly discouraged. The IVT report should include the following sections: 1. Executive summary. 2. List of abbreviations. 3. Introduction, detailing the request for verification, dates and details of the country visit, and the composition of the IVT. 4. Methodology used by the IVT to verify the country’s claims. 5. Activities, including a daily account of meetings, individuals met, and in-country movements. 6. Critical discussion of the interventions carried out by the country to control and eliminate onchocerciasis, with a focus on monitoring and evaluation activities. 7. Conclusions, where the IVT assesses the compliance of the data with WHO’s elimination criteria and provides its opinion on whether the verification process should be considered successful. 8. Recommendations to the country, focusing on post-elimination surveillance if verification is successful, or on steps needed to meet elimination goals if verification is unsuccessful or inconclusive due to incomplete data. 9. References, with full citations for any published literature cited in the report. The effects of ivermectin distribution on parasite transmission can be evaluated by monitoring the infection rates of black flies with larvae of Onchocerca volvulus. This method has several advantages over parasitological evaluation of the human population, particularly when children are involved: Infection rates in black flies are rapid and sensitive indicators of changes in community microfilarial load resulting from ivermectin distribution. Changes in vector infection rates correlate well with the percentage coverage of the human population with ivermectin. The absence of infective-stage larvae in the vector population during the transmission season is the first indicator of interrupted parasite transmission. Monitoring very low vector infection rates using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and DNA technology is easier and less expensive than monitoring low levels of infection in children. The use of O. volvulus-specific DNA probes ensures absolute specificity and allows for processing large numbers of black flies, increasing the reliability of results. Vector collection teams working in the community can deliver health messages about ivermectin, thereby increasing coverage. The process is completely non-invasive and well-accepted by the community. For pre-treatment baseline data, vector infection rates should ideally be measured over a complete year or at least a full transmission season. This provides baseline data for comparison with post-treatment evaluations. The collection methodology can also be used to investigate areas that might be susceptible to parasite introduction. Systematic collections determine whether a competent vector is present and if the biting density is high enough to support a transmission cycle. PCR technology is recommended over dissection for monitoring the effects of larviciding or ivermectin in trials, as dissection of large numbers of black flies is technically and financially challenging. PCR testing involves grouping fly collections into pools and testing for O. volvulus larvae. Maximum pool sizes vary by species and DNA purification methods. If no positive pools are detected, the upper bound of the 95% confidence interval for the annual transmission potential (ATP) will be within acceptable limits. Data are analyzed using statistical software such as PoolScreen, developed by the University of Alabama and the University of South Florida. In the laboratory, flies are examined under a stereomicroscope, identified by species, and grouped into pools. Heads and bodies are tested separately, as most infective-stage larvae are found in the head. Testing bodies is important for surveillance of renewed transmission, as a positive result indicates previous contact with a microfilaria-positive person. If evidence of parasite-vector contact is detected, all heads must be tested to estimate the prevalence of L3 larvae in the flies. Both approaches—testing heads only or testing both heads and bodies—are operationally feasible and provide valuable data for assessing transmission interruption.
